opus-5.5.text:
Sydney's paper has been really useful for me because it gives a nice account of why we have norms at all, and how we can step outside them when they stop serving us.

The core idea, as I understand it, is that the ideal of contractualism is that the right thing to do is whatever everyone affected would agree to if they could actually sit down and bargain it out. But we almost never have time for that. Actually simulating a negotiation among everyone involved is very expensive. So what humans do instead is use a range of cheaper approximations. At one end you have rules and norms, which are cached answers to what we'd probably agree on in typical situations. In the middle you have things like virtual bargaining, where you quickly simulate what the other party would accept. And at the far end you have explicit negotiation, or real deliberation, when the stakes justify the cost.

What I find compelling is that this framing makes norms *answerable* to something. A norm isn't just a brute fact about what's done around here. It's a compression of a hypothetical agreement, and like any compression, it can be lossy. It can be tuned to circumstances that no longer hold, or it can reflect agreements where some people were never really at the table. So when you notice a norm producing outcomes that clearly wouldn't survive the "could everyone reasonably accept this?" test, that's a signal to move up the resource ladder: stop relying on the cached rule, and actually do the more expensive reasoning about what people would agree to.

That's how I think about reasoning our way out of bad norms. It's not that you throw out norms. They're incredibly valuable, and most of the time following them is the rational thing to do given limited time and information. But you need some meta-level sensitivity to when the rule has drifted from its justification. Children do this, actually. They learn a rule, then at some point they figure out it doesn't apply in a weird edge case, because they've grasped what the rule was *for*.

For AI, this matters a lot. A lot of alignment work implicitly treats norms or preferences as fixed targets to imitate. If you take the resource-rational contractualist view seriously, what you want is a system that understands norms as approximations of mutual agreement. It should be able to follow them efficiently, but it should also recognize when it's in a situation where the norm misfires and it needs to reason more carefully about the interests of everyone affected. It also suggests a picture of moral progress that's neither pure conservatism nor "the AI computes the true morality from scratch." It's more like iterative renegotiation, which is what I think healthy human societies do anyway.

The open question, which I think about a lot, is who gets counted in the hypothetical bargain, and how you avoid the approximation just smuggling in the existing power structure. If your virtual bargaining model of other people is itself learned from biased norms, you can end up ratifying the status quo. So I see Sydney's framework less as a solution and more as the right shape for the problem. It tells you what the norms are trying to track, which is what lets you notice when they've gone wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes norms as cached approximations of hypothetical agreement and virtual bargaining as a way to simulate what others would accept, with more deliberation when needed. This conveys how people use bargaining to guide what norms or actions should be.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Sydney's paper has been really generative for me, partly because it gives a vocabulary for something I'd been circling around for a while. The basic idea of resource-rational contractualism is that the ideal of morality is something like: what would everyone affected agree to, if they could all sit down and bargain it out? But of course nobody can actually do that in real time. You don't convene the parliament of all stakeholders every time you decide whether to hold the door open for someone. So we have this hierarchy of cheaper approximations. At the bottom you have norms and rules, just cached outcomes of past agreements. Above that you have things like simulating what the relevant parties would say, or doing a rough utilitarian tally. And at the top you have actual negotiation and consensus-building, which is expensive but the most faithful to the ideal.

What I find clarifying about that framing is that it tells you when norms are supposed to be revisable. A norm isn't sacred, it's a compression of a contract. And compressions fail. The world changes, the set of stakeholders changes, or you realize the original agreement was made under conditions where some parties weren't at the table at all. So the question of "how do we reason our way out of a bad norm" becomes: when do you pay the cost to decompress? When is it worth climbing up the hierarchy and actually re-asking what people would agree to?

And I think that connects to how I've been thinking about AI systems that are supposed to follow norms. If you build an agent that just learns and enforces the existing normative equilibrium, you've built something that's really good at the cheap layer and has no mechanism for the expensive one. It'll faithfully reproduce whatever conventions it was trained on, including the ones that were only ever stable because the people they harmed couldn't object. So part of what Sydney's work pushed me toward is thinking about norm-following not as the end state but as a default that has to be defeasible, where the agent has some model of why the norm exists and some sense of the conditions under which that justification stops holding.

The honest caveat is that this doesn't tell you how to do the hard part. Knowing that you should sometimes escalate to a more deliberative mode doesn't tell you what the right agreement is once you get there, and it doesn't resolve disagreements about who counts as a stakeholder. But I think it correctly locates the problem. Bad norms aren't usually bad because people are being irrational. They're bad because the cheap approximation drifted from the thing it was approximating, and nobody was paying attention to the gap.

r001.rationale: The response describes moral norms as approximations of what affected parties would agree to through bargaining, including simulated deliberation as a cheaper approximation to actual negotiation.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling about resource-rational contractualism is that it connects two things we sometimes treat as separate: trying to justify our actions to other people, and needing practical rules that we can actually live by with limited time and cognitive resources.

Rules are useful partly because we can’t deliberate about every consequence of every action. But that also means a rule can persist after we’ve forgotten its justification, or because we’ve never seriously considered the perspective of the people it harms. So the fact that a norm is widely accepted doesn’t settle whether it’s defensible.

The contractualist move is to ask: could we justify this arrangement to each of the people affected by it? Whose objections have we left out? That gives us a way to scrutinize the norm rather than just reproduce it. And the resource-rational part asks how we turn that scrutiny into something people can realistically use—a better rule, or a clearer sense of when to stop following the default and think harder.

That’s the connection to reasoning our way out of bad norms for me. Reasoning isn’t just applying the rules we already have. It can also mean examining why we have those rules, bringing excluded perspectives into the discussion, and revising them.

r001.rationale: The response describes asking whether an arrangement can be justified to each affected person, but it does not characterize the account as using virtual bargaining to determine moral norms.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find compelling about Sydney’s work is that it treats moral reasoning as something we do with limited time and computational resources. We can’t work out every consequence of every action, so we need rules. But those rules can also become entrenched in ways that are harmful.

Resource-rational contractualism gives us a way to think about both sides of that. We can ask: What rules could people reasonably agree to, taking into account that they have to actually understand and use them? And when a norm goes wrong, we can step back and ask whether the people affected by it would accept it, rather than treating its existence as a justification.

That’s the sense in which reasoning might help us get out of bad norms. We inherit these relatively efficient ways of coordinating, but we also have the capacity to reflect on them and propose alternatives. The hard part is making that reflection sensitive to everyone’s perspective, including people whose interests the existing norm has made easy to overlook.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasonable agreement on usable rules and reconsidering norms from affected people’s perspectives, but it does not describe virtual bargaining as the means of determining moral norms.
